title: Four meanings, one phrase
summary: What “quantum oncology” covers — computing, sensing, quantum biology and pseudoscience — the scale of cancer, and how this course grades every claim.

shots.title:
Quantum
oncology.
shots.subtitle: One phrase, four meanings — and one of them can kill.
shots.narration: You already know quantum computing. This course teaches you cancer, then puts the two together carefully enough to publish.

shots.label: new cancer cases worldwide in 2022
shots.narration: Start with the scale. In 2022 there were close to twenty million new cancer cases worldwide, and nine point seven million cancer deaths.

shots.text: About **one in five** people develop cancer in their lifetime; about one in nine men and one in twelve women die from it.
shots.narration: About one in five people develop cancer in their lifetime. Around one in nine men and one in twelve women die from it.

shots.text: Lung cancer: the most diagnosed (**~2.5 million**) and the deadliest (**~1.8 million**). Cases are projected to reach **~35 million a year by 2050** (an estimate).
shots.narration: Lung cancer was both the most diagnosed cancer, almost two and a half million cases, and the deadliest, about one point eight million deaths. Demographic projections put new cases at about thirty-five million a year by 2050.

shots.heading: “Quantum oncology” can mean
shots.narration: The phrase covers four different things: quantum computing for cancer research, quantum sensing and imaging, speculative quantum biology, and pseudoscience sold to patients.

shots.text: This course is mostly about the **first**, with a lesson on the second and third — and a warning about the fourth.
shots.narration: This course is mostly about the first. One lesson covers sensing and quantum biology. And the fourth gets a warning, because it does real harm.

shots.label: the risk of death when alternative medicine replaced conventional treatment
shots.context: US cohort, curable cancers · hazard ratio 2.50 (95% CI 1.88–3.27)
shots.narration: In a US study of curable cancers, patients who chose alternative medicine instead of conventional treatment had two and a half times the risk of death.
Here is the route: cancer biology, the clinic and its evidence, the classical computation you must beat, quantum methods, the field today, and research practice — ending in your own proposal.

shots.text: Every factual sentence links to the ledger: **sourced, dated and graded** — verified, derived, estimate or contested.
shots.narration: Every factual sentence links to a ledger entry with its sources, the date it was checked, and a grade: verified, derived, estimate or contested. Use the same discipline in your papers.

shots.text: The deep reason to care: to simulate **quantum** nature, use a **quantum** computer. Drug molecules are quantum systems. Tumours are not.
shots.narration: The deepest reason to care was given in 1982, when Richard Feynman argued that simulating quantum physics efficiently needs a quantum computer. Drug molecules are quantum systems. Tumours, as a whole, are not.

shots.text: Homework starts now: write down **where you're starting from**.
shots.narration: Your first piece of homework starts now: a short note on where you are starting from. It becomes the first page of your research proposal.

steps.title: Which kind of quantum oncology?
steps.brief: Sort each statement by what kind of “quantum oncology” it is. The last bucket is for claims a patient should walk away from.

cards.text: A 16-qubit circuit supplies the prior of a generative model that proposes KRAS inhibitors.
cards.why: A quantum circuit Born machine on an IBM processor fed a classical model (Nature Biotechnology, 2025).

cards.text: Phase estimation could compute the electronic structure of cytochrome P450, the enzyme family that breaks down drugs such as imatinib.
cards.why: A resource estimate for a fault-tolerant computer.

cards.text: A quantum annealer optimises radiotherapy beam intensities.
cards.why: First tried in 2015 on two prostate cases.

cards.text: Fluorescent nanodiamonds, modulated with microwaves, make a lateral-flow test far more sensitive.
cards.why: The quantum spin states of nitrogen-vacancy defects are used to separate signal from background.

cards.text: Hyperpolarised pyruvate MRI shows tumour metabolism in men with prostate cancer.
cards.why: Nuclear spin polarisation boosts the MRI signal; first done in patients in 2013.

cards.text: Protons tunnelling across DNA base pairs may create mutation-prone tautomers.
cards.why: Proposed in 1963 and modelled in 2022, but not measured in cells.

cards.text: A clinic offers “quantum frequency healing” instead of chemotherapy.
cards.why: Replacing treatment with alternative medicine was linked to 2.5× the risk of death.

cards.text: A “quantum energy” bracelet is sold to shrink tumours.
cards.why: No mechanism, no evidence — the word “quantum” is the product.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many new cancer cases were there worldwide in 2022?
questions.explain: GLOBOCAN estimates close to 20 million new cases and 9.7 million deaths in 2022.

questions.prompt: Which cancer was both the most diagnosed and the leading cause of cancer death worldwide in 2022?
questions.explain: Lung: almost 2.5 million cases (12.4%) and about 1.8 million deaths (18.7%).

questions.prompt: Which of these is quantum sensing rather than quantum computing?
questions.explain: Hyperpolarisation manipulates nuclear spins to boost an imaging signal; no computation is quantum.

questions.prompt: In this course's ledger, what does “contested” mean?
options: A primary source makes it, but credible parties dispute it or it rests only on preprints — the note explains the dispute
The claim is a projection about the future
questions.explain: Projections are “estimate”. “Contested” keeps a disputed claim visible, with the dispute written out — exactly what a careful paper does.
